overview: Union in PySpark vertically stacks the rows of two or more DataFrames into one, appending the rows of the second DataFrame below the first.

`union` (and its alias `unionAll`) combines DataFrames strictly by column POSITION, while `unionByName` combines them by column NAME, which is the key distinction that prevents silent data corruption.
Union does NOT remove duplicates -- it is a UNION ALL by default; you must call `distinct()` (or `dropDuplicates()`) afterward to deduplicate.
learningObjectives: Distinguish `union` (position-based) from `unionByName` (name-based) and recognize the column-order pitfall that corrupts data with `union`.
Understand schema compatibility requirements, the `allowMissingColumns` option, and how Spark resolves columns when schemas differ.
Know that union does not deduplicate and how to combine many DataFrames correctly and efficiently.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: Union is a set-style transformation that returns a new DataFrame containing all rows from the input DataFrames concatenated together. `DataFrame.union(other)` resolves columns by ordinal position and requires the same number of columns with compatible types. `DataFrame.unionByName(other, allowMissingColumns=False)` resolves columns by name, optionally filling absent columns with null when `allowMissingColumns=True`. Neither method removes duplicate rows; both implement SQL UNION ALL semantics.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: Union is like taping two spreadsheets together top-to-bottom to make one taller spreadsheet. `union` lines them up by column position -- the 1st column of one goes under the 1st column of the other, regardless of the headers -- so if the columns are in a different order you silently mix data. `unionByName` lines them up by the column headers, so name matches name even if the order differs. Either way, if the same row appears in both, you get it twice unless you explicitly de-duplicate.
coreConcept.historicalContext: Early Spark only offered `union`/`unionAll` with strict positional, UNION ALL semantics inherited from RDDs and SQL, which frequently caused subtle data-mixing bugs when schemas were in different orders. `unionByName` was added in Spark 2.3 to resolve columns by name, and the `allowMissingColumns` parameter arrived in Spark 3.1 to gracefully handle schema evolution where one DataFrame has extra or missing columns. `unionAll` was deprecated as a redundant alias of `union`.

whyItMatters.business: Combining data from multiple sources (regions, days, partners) into a single dataset underpins consolidated reporting; a positional-union bug can silently swap fields like revenue and cost, producing wrong financials.
whyItMatters.engineering: Union is the workhorse for stitching together partitioned reads, backfills, and incremental loads; choosing union vs unionByName correctly is a frequent source of hard-to-debug data quality incidents.
whyItMatters.scalability: Union itself is a cheap narrow transformation (no shuffle), but careless patterns -- like unioning hundreds of DataFrames one at a time or adding distinct() unnecessarily -- introduce expensive plans and shuffles.
whyItMatters.cost: Avoiding an unnecessary distinct() after union saves a full shuffle; understanding UNION ALL semantics prevents both wasted dedup work and the cost of fixing corrupted downstream data.
whyItMatters.reliability: Name-based resolution and schema-compatibility awareness prevent silent column misalignment, which is one of the most damaging and hardest-to-detect data reliability failures.

coreComponents.name: union (positional)
coreComponents.definition: Combines two DataFrames by matching columns on ordinal position; requires the same number of columns with type-compatible positions.
coreComponents.purpose: Append rows when both DataFrames are guaranteed to have identical column order and schema.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Concatenate rows positionally without renaming or reordering columns; the result keeps the left DataFrame's column names.

coreComponents.name: unionByName (name-based)
coreComponents.definition: Combines DataFrames by matching columns on name rather than position, optionally tolerating missing columns.
coreComponents.purpose: Append rows safely when column order may differ or schemas have evolved.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Align columns by name, fill missing columns with null when allowed, and raise an error on incompatible/unknown columns when not allowed.

coreComponents.name: distinct / dropDuplicates (post-union dedup)
coreComponents.definition: Transformations applied after union to remove duplicate rows, since union keeps all rows (UNION ALL).
coreComponents.purpose: Convert UNION ALL behavior into SQL UNION (distinct rows) when deduplication is required.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Trigger a shuffle to group and drop duplicate rows; `dropDuplicates(subset)` dedups on a key subset.

internalWorking: Union is a logical `Union` node in Catalyst whose children are the input plans; at execution it concatenates partitions from each child, so the result partition count is the sum of the inputs' partitions -- no shuffle is required.
`union` performs analysis-time validation that the children have the same number of columns and type-compatible columns by ordinal position; it does NOT check or align column names.
`unionByName` rewrites each child by projecting/reordering columns to a common name-aligned schema before the Union node, so positionally different schemas are correctly aligned by name.
With `allowMissingColumns=True`, unionByName adds the union of all column names to each side, inserting literal nulls for columns a given DataFrame lacks.
Because union keeps every row, deduplication (distinct/dropDuplicates) is a separate transformation that introduces an aggregation/shuffle stage after the cheap union.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: DataFrame A (rows, schema_A) + DataFrame B (rows, schema_B) -> [union: align by position | unionByName: align by name (+nulls for missing if allowed)] -> Combined DataFrame (A rows then B rows) -> [optional distinct/dropDuplicates -> shuffle] -> Deduplicated DataFrame
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. DataFrame A has columns (id, name, amount); DataFrame B has columns (id, amount, name) -- same names, different order.
2. `A.union(B)` aligns by position: B's `amount` lands under A's `name`, and B's `name` under A's `amount` -- silent corruption.
3. `A.unionByName(B)` aligns by name: id->id, name->name, amount->amount, producing correct rows regardless of order.
4. The Union node concatenates partitions from A and then B; no shuffle occurs and the combined partition count equals the sum.
5. If duplicates must be removed, an explicit `.distinct()` triggers a shuffle to drop repeated rows.

keyTerminology.meaning: Combining all rows from inputs without removing duplicates.
keyTerminology.importance: PySpark `union`/`unionByName` are UNION ALL by default, so you must add distinct() to get SQL UNION (distinct) behavior.

keyTerminology.meaning: Matching columns by their index/order rather than by name.
keyTerminology.importance: It is how `union` works and is the source of the column-order pitfall.

keyTerminology.meaning: Matching columns by their names so order does not matter.
keyTerminology.importance: It is how `unionByName` works and is the safe default for evolving or differently ordered schemas.

keyTerminology.meaning: A unionByName flag (Spark 3.1+) that fills columns absent in one side with null instead of failing.
keyTerminology.importance: Enables unioning DataFrames with non-identical schemas during schema evolution.

importantConcepts.explanation: `union` ignores column names entirely and matches by position. If two DataFrames have the same column names in a different order, `union` will silently place values under the wrong column, corrupting data without raising an error. `unionByName` avoids this by matching on names.

Both `union` and `unionByName` keep all rows (UNION ALL). Duplicate rows from overlapping sources will appear multiple times; call `distinct()` or `dropDuplicates()` afterward when dedup is required, accepting the extra shuffle cost.

Chaining many pairwise unions builds a deep logical plan. Prefer reducing a list with `functools.reduce(DataFrame.unionByName, dfs)` or reading all sources in one call (e.g., a glob path) so Spark builds a flat, efficient Union plan instead of a deeply nested one.

variationsAndTypes: **union / unionAll:** Positional concatenation; unionAll is a deprecated alias of union.
**unionByName:** Name-based concatenation requiring matching column names.
**unionByName(allowMissingColumns=True):** Name-based concatenation that null-fills columns absent on either side.
**union + distinct:** Emulates SQL UNION (distinct rows) by adding a dedup shuffle.
**reduce(unionByName, [...]):** Combining a list of many DataFrames into one flat union.
advantages: **No shuffle:** Union is a narrow transformation -- it simply concatenates partitions, making it cheap.
**Schema-safe option:** unionByName aligns by name, eliminating the column-order corruption risk.
**Schema-evolution friendly:** allowMissingColumns lets you combine DataFrames whose schemas differ slightly.
**Composable:** Easily reduces a list of DataFrames into one combined dataset for backfills and multi-source loads.
disadvantages: **Positional trap:** Plain union silently mixes data when column order differs and names are ignored.
**No dedup:** Duplicates persist unless you add an explicit, shuffle-heavy distinct().
**Strict schema needs:** union requires identical column counts and compatible types, failing otherwise.
**Plan bloat:** Naive pairwise unioning of many DataFrames can create deep, slow-to-analyze plans.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Use `union` only when you are certain both DataFrames share identical column order and schema (e.g., reading partitions of the same table). Use `unionByName` whenever schemas may differ in order or evolve over time; add distinct() only when deduplication is genuinely required.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid `union` (positional) when combining DataFrames from heterogeneous sources or after transformations that may reorder columns. Avoid adding distinct() if sources are known to be non-overlapping, since it adds an unnecessary shuffle.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: Merging guest lists from two events: `union` is like stapling the two lists together blindly by column position -- if one list has columns (Name, Phone) and the other (Phone, Name), you end up with phone numbers in the name column. `unionByName` reads the headers and matches Name-to-Name and Phone-to-Phone. And because it is UNION ALL, anyone invited to both events appears twice unless you de-duplicate.

commonMisconceptions.myth: union matches columns by name like SQL UNION.
commonMisconceptions.reality: PySpark `union` matches by position, not name. SQL-style UNION semantics on names require `unionByName`. The positional behavior is a frequent cause of silent data corruption.

commonMisconceptions.myth: union removes duplicate rows like SQL UNION.
commonMisconceptions.reality: PySpark union is UNION ALL -- it keeps duplicates. You must explicitly call distinct()/dropDuplicates() to remove them.
`unionAll` is just a deprecated alias of `union`; both are positional UNION ALL. Neither performs deduplication.

productionConsiderations.scalability: Union scales well because it adds no shuffle, but the result partition count is the sum of inputs; after many unions consider `coalesce`/`repartition` to right-size partitions before downstream wide operations.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Prefer unionByName to eliminate column-order corruption; validate that schemas are compatible and document expected columns to catch schema drift early.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: Union is a deterministic narrow transformation; failed tasks recompute their single input partition cheaply without recomputing the whole union.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Watch for unexpected row counts after union (duplicates) and for added shuffle stages when distinct() is applied; monitor schema mismatches surfaced at analysis time.
productionConsiderations.security: Union introduces no new security surface beyond the inputs; ensure all source DataFrames share the same access/governance controls so combining does not leak restricted columns.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Skip distinct() when sources are non-overlapping, flatten many-DataFrame unions with reduce or glob reads, and coalesce afterward to avoid an explosion of tiny partitions that raise scheduling overhead.
productionConsiderations.performance: The expensive part is rarely the union itself but a following distinct()/dropDuplicates() shuffle or an inflated partition count; tune those rather than the union.

codeExamples.title: The column-order trap: union vs unionByName
codeExamples.overview: Show how positional union silently corrupts data when column order differs, and how unionByName fixes it.
codeExamples.code:
import pyspark.sql.functions as F

# Same column NAMES, different ORDER
df_a = spark.createDataFrame([(1, "Alice", 100)], ["id", "name", "amount"])
df_b = spark.createDataFrame([(2, 50, "Bob")],   ["id", "amount", "name"])

# union matches by POSITION -> amount and name get swapped for df_b's row!
bad = df_a.union(df_b)
bad.show()

# unionByName matches by NAME -> columns align correctly
good = df_a.unionByName(df_b)
good.show()
codeExamples.breakdown: `df_a` and `df_b` have identical column names but different order. `union` aligns the 2nd column of each (name vs amount) and the 3rd (amount vs name), so df_b's row is corrupted. `unionByName` matches id->id, name->name, amount->amount regardless of order, producing correct rows.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Using union after a select/derivation that changed column order; the job runs without error but data is silently mixed. Type coercion may even hide the swap when types are compatible.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Default to unionByName for any DataFrames not guaranteed to share identical column order; reserve positional union for partitions of the exact same table.

codeExamples.title: unionByName with allowMissingColumns for schema evolution
codeExamples.overview: Combine DataFrames whose schemas differ by null-filling missing columns.
codeExamples.code:
import pyspark.sql.functions as F

# Old schema lacks the new 'channel' column
df_old = spark.createDataFrame([(1, "Alice")], ["id", "name"])
df_new = spark.createDataFrame([(2, "Bob", "web")], ["id", "name", "channel"])

# allowMissingColumns null-fills 'channel' for the old rows
combined = df_old.unionByName(df_new, allowMissingColumns=True)
combined.show()
codeExamples.breakdown: `df_old` is missing the `channel` column present in `df_new`. With `allowMissingColumns=True`, unionByName forms the union of column names and inserts null for `channel` in the old rows. Without this flag the call raises an analysis exception about the unresolved column.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Forgetting that allowMissingColumns requires Spark 3.1+; assuming plain union can handle missing columns (it cannot -- it requires equal column counts).
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Use allowMissingColumns deliberately for known schema evolution; otherwise keep schemas strict so unexpected drift fails loudly instead of being silently null-filled.

codeExamples.title: Union does not dedup; combining many DataFrames efficiently
codeExamples.overview: Demonstrate UNION ALL behavior and a flat reduce over a list of DataFrames.
codeExamples.code:
from functools import reduce
from pyspark.sql import DataFrame
import pyspark.sql.functions as F

d1 = spark.createDataFrame([(1, "a")], ["id", "v"])
d2 = spark.createDataFrame([(1, "a"), (2, "b")], ["id", "v"])

# UNION ALL: the (1, 'a') row appears twice
all_rows = d1.unionByName(d2)
print("with dups:", all_rows.count())          # 3

# Add distinct() to remove duplicates (incurs a shuffle)
print("distinct:", all_rows.distinct().count()) # 2

# Flatten a list of many DataFrames into one union
dfs = [d1, d2, d1]
combined = reduce(DataFrame.unionByName, dfs)
print("combined:", combined.count())            # 5
codeExamples.breakdown: `unionByName` keeps the duplicate (1,'a') so the count is 3, confirming UNION ALL. `.distinct()` removes duplicates at the cost of a shuffle. `reduce(DataFrame.unionByName, dfs)` folds a list into one combined DataFrame, producing a flat Union plan instead of manually chaining calls.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Expecting union to behave like SQL UNION and dedup automatically; chaining unions in a Python loop that rebuilds the plan repeatedly and bloats the logical plan.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Only add distinct() when sources actually overlap. For many same-schema sources, read them in a single call (glob path) so Spark plans one scan instead of many unions.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: A retailer ingests daily sales extracts from three regional systems. One region recently added a `loyalty_tier` column and another exports columns in a different order. The data team must consolidate all regions into a single deduplicated daily sales table without silently mixing fields.
endToEndExample.inputData: Three DataFrames: `east(order_id, customer_id, amount)`, `west(amount, order_id, customer_id)` (different column order), and `north(order_id, customer_id, amount, loyalty_tier)` (extra column). Some order_ids overlap between regions due to a shared returns feed.
endToEndExample.architecture: Spark reads the three regional Parquet extracts, aligns them with unionByName + allowMissingColumns, deduplicates on order_id, and writes a single consolidated Parquet table.
processingSteps: 1. Read the three regional extracts into DataFrames east, west, north.
2. Combine with `reduce(lambda a, b: a.unionByName(b, allowMissingColumns=True), [east, west, north])` so columns align by name and `loyalty_tier` is null-filled for east/west.
3. Confirm row count equals the sum of inputs (UNION ALL keeps duplicates).
5. Coalesce to a sensible partition count to avoid tiny files, then write the consolidated table.
6. Validate the final schema contains the superset of columns with correct alignment.
endToEndExample.output: A single consolidated sales DataFrame with correctly name-aligned columns, `loyalty_tier` populated only where available (null elsewhere), and duplicate returns removed.
endToEndExample.monitoring: Compare pre-dedup and post-dedup row counts to quantify overlap; assert the output schema matches the expected superset; alert if any region's schema drifts unexpectedly (e.g., a renamed column appears as an unexpected null-filled field).
endToEndExample.errorHandling: Without allowMissingColumns the union would raise an analysis exception on the missing `loyalty_tier`; the flag handles known evolution. A guard checks that all expected core columns (order_id, customer_id, amount) are present in every source before unioning so a renamed column fails loudly rather than producing nulls.
endToEndExample.finalResult: A reliable, deduplicated daily sales table that correctly merges regions despite different column order and schema evolution -- avoiding the classic positional-union corruption while paying the dedup shuffle cost only once at the end.

industryUseCases.problem: Consolidating daily sales extracts from regional systems that have different column order and evolving schemas.
industryUseCases.solution: Use `unionByName(allowMissingColumns=True)` to align by name and null-fill new columns, then dropDuplicates on the order key.
industryUseCases.benefits: Prevents field mix-ups from positional union, tolerates schema evolution, and produces one clean consolidated table.

industryUseCases.problem: Combining a historical backfill DataFrame with incremental daily loads that share a schema.
industryUseCases.solution: Fold all daily DataFrames with `reduce(DataFrame.unionByName, dfs)` into a flat union, deduplicating only on overlapping boundary dates.
industryUseCases.benefits: A single efficient Union plan, minimal shuffle (dedup only where needed), and safe name-based alignment.

industryUseCases.problem: Merging event streams from multiple ingestion jobs where some sources include extra optional attributes.
industryUseCases.solution: unionByName with allowMissingColumns to unify the superset schema, keeping all events (UNION ALL) for downstream aggregation.
industryUseCases.benefits: No premature deduplication, correct column alignment, and a consistent superset schema for analytics.

productionDeepDive.scalability: Union adds no shuffle and scales linearly, but the output partition count is the sum of inputs. After unioning many sources, the partition count can explode and create scheduling overhead; coalesce or repartition before heavy downstream operations.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: As a narrow transformation, union recomputes only the affected input partition on task failure. Adding distinct() introduces a shuffle stage whose shuffle files enable standard task retries.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: Union does not stress the cluster on its own; the risk to shared clusters comes from a following distinct()/dropDuplicates() shuffle. Schedule dedup-heavy consolidation jobs in appropriate scheduler pools.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Union is deterministic for the same inputs, so re-running reproduces identical combined data. Deduplication via dropDuplicates is also deterministic on the chosen key subset, aiding reproducible recovery.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Prefer unionByName for safety; avoid unnecessary distinct(); flatten many-DataFrame unions with reduce or a single glob read; coalesce post-union to control partition count. Push filters before the union so each branch scans less data (Catalyst can also push some predicates).
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: The biggest cost lever is avoiding an unneeded dedup shuffle and preventing tiny-partition explosion. Read homogeneous sources with one call rather than many unions to minimize planning and scan overhead.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Ensure all unioned sources share the same data classification and access controls; combining a restricted source with an open one can broaden exposure. allowMissingColumns null-fills rather than dropping, so it will not leak by omission but can mask missing-data issues.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Track input vs output row counts to detect unexpected duplicates, watch the SQL plan for an added Exchange when distinct() is used, and assert the resulting schema matches the expected superset to catch silent drift.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Validate that name-based alignment produced the expected columns, that null-fills only occur where schema evolution is expected, and that dedup keys are correct. A positional-union bug typically shows up as type/value anomalies in specific columns.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Log per-source row counts and the final consolidated count; alert on schema mismatches at analysis time and on dedup ratios outside expected bounds (signaling unexpected overlap or duplication).

recommendedPractices: **Default to unionByName** for any DataFrames not guaranteed to share identical column order, eliminating the positional corruption risk.
**Add distinct()/dropDuplicates() only when needed**, since union is UNION ALL and dedup costs a shuffle.
**Use allowMissingColumns intentionally** for known schema evolution, not as a blanket way to silence schema mismatches.
**Flatten many-DataFrame unions** with `reduce(DataFrame.unionByName, dfs)` or a single glob read to keep the plan flat and efficient.
engineeringStandards: Validate that all expected core columns exist in every source before unioning so renamed/missing columns fail loudly.
Reserve positional `union` strictly for partitions of the exact same table with guaranteed identical schema.
Document whether a consolidation step deduplicates and on which key subset.
designRecommendations: Coalesce or repartition after combining many sources to avoid an explosion of tiny partitions.
Push filters before the union so each input branch scans and carries less data.
Define an explicit target superset schema and align sources to it rather than relying on incidental column ordering.
namingConventions: Name combined DataFrames to reflect their content and dedup state, e.g., `sales_all_regions_dedup`.
When a DataFrame is a raw UNION ALL with possible duplicates, encode it (e.g., `events_union_all`) so downstream code does not assume distinctness.
documentationStandards: Document the union method used (position vs name) and why, especially when allowMissingColumns is enabled.
Record the expected superset schema and the deduplication key for consolidated datasets.
Note any schema-evolution assumptions baked into the union step.
testingStrategies: Unit-test union vs unionByName on DataFrames with deliberately reordered columns to assert correct alignment.
Test allowMissingColumns null-fill behavior and that disallowed mismatches raise the expected analysis error.
Assert post-union counts and dedup counts on overlapping fixtures to verify UNION ALL and distinct() behavior.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using positional union when column order differs.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Developers assume union aligns by name like SQL, or a prior select/derivation changed column order unnoticed.
commonMistakes.impact: Values land under the wrong columns silently -- no error is raised -- corrupting downstream analytics and reports.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Use `unionByName` so columns are matched by name regardless of order; reserve positional union for identical-schema partitions.

commonMistakes.whyItHappens: SQL UNION removes duplicates, so engineers assume PySpark union does too.
commonMistakes.impact: Duplicate rows from overlapping sources persist, inflating counts and skewing aggregations.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Remember union is UNION ALL; add `.distinct()` or `.dropDuplicates(subset)` explicitly when dedup is required.

commonMistakes.mistake: Chaining many unions in a Python loop, bloating the plan.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: It feels natural to accumulate `result = result.union(df)` inside a loop over many sources.
commonMistakes.impact: A deeply nested logical plan slows analysis/optimization and can create an excessive number of partitions.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Use `reduce(DataFrame.unionByName, dfs)` for a flat plan, or read all same-schema sources in one call, then coalesce.

comparisonSection.explanation: union matches columns strictly by ordinal position and ignores names, so differently ordered schemas silently misalign. unionByName matches columns by name, so column order does not matter and data stays correctly aligned.

union requires the same number of type-compatible columns and fails otherwise. unionByName with allowMissingColumns null-fills columns absent on either side, enabling safe combination across schema evolution.

By default both union and unionByName keep all rows including duplicates (UNION ALL, no shuffle). Adding distinct()/dropDuplicates() removes duplicates but introduces a shuffle, matching SQL UNION (distinct) semantics.

beginnerQuestions.question: Does PySpark's union remove duplicate rows?
beginnerQuestions.answer: No. PySpark `union` (and `unionByName`) is UNION ALL -- it keeps all rows including duplicates. To remove duplicates you must call `distinct()` or `dropDuplicates()`.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: A common SQL-versus-Spark gotcha; interviewers check you do not assume SQL UNION dedup behavior.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is the difference between union and unionAll in PySpark?
beginnerQuestions.answer: They are the same -- `unionAll` is a deprecated alias of `union`. Both perform positional UNION ALL with no deduplication.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Tests awareness that unionAll is legacy and identical in behavior to union.

intermediateQuestions.question: What is the difference between union and unionByName, and why does it matter?
intermediateQuestions.answer: `union` matches columns by position; `unionByName` matches by name. It matters because if two DataFrames have the same column names in a different order, union silently places values under the wrong columns and corrupts data, whereas unionByName aligns them correctly.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: This is the central union interview question; the answer must call out the silent column-order corruption.

intermediateQuestions.question: How do you union two DataFrames whose schemas are not identical?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Use `unionByName(other, allowMissingColumns=True)` (Spark 3.1+), which aligns by name and null-fills columns missing from either side. Plain union would fail because it requires identical column counts.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Tests knowledge of allowMissingColumns and schema-evolution handling.

intermediateQuestions.question: Does union trigger a shuffle?
intermediateQuestions.answer: No. Union is a narrow transformation that simply concatenates partitions, so it does not shuffle. A following distinct()/dropDuplicates() does trigger a shuffle.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Distinguishes the cheap union from the costly dedup step that often follows it.

advancedQuestions.question: How does Catalyst represent unionByName with allowMissingColumns internally?
advancedQuestions.answer: Catalyst rewrites each child plan with a projection that reorders/aligns columns by name and adds literal-null columns for any names missing from that child, producing a common schema before the logical Union node. Plain union has no such rewrite and validates only column count and positional type compatibility.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Shows understanding of how name resolution is implemented as projections in the logical plan.

advancedQuestions.question: What is the efficient way to union a list of 200 same-schema DataFrames, and why?
advancedQuestions.answer: Use `reduce(DataFrame.unionByName, dfs)` to build a single flat Union node, or better, read all sources in one DataFrameReader call with a glob path. Iteratively chaining unions in a loop builds a deep nested plan that is slow to analyze and can produce an excessive partition count.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Tests plan-shape awareness and the practical pattern for many-source consolidation.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: After a deploy, a daily consolidation job runs without errors but revenue numbers are wildly wrong. The job unions three regional DataFrames. What do you investigate first?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: No error but wrong values suggests silent misalignment. The job uses positional `union`; one region likely emits columns in a different order after a recent change. Check each source's column order and switch to unionByName.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Inspect each region's column order; a positional `union` will swap fields when order differs. Replace `union` with `unionByName` (adding allowMissingColumns if schemas evolved) so columns align by name, then re-validate revenue.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design a consolidation layer that merges daily extracts from N partner sources with slightly different and evolving schemas into one deduplicated table.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Define a target superset schema. For each source, validate core columns then align via unionByName(allowMissingColumns=True). Fold all sources with reduce into one flat union, dropDuplicates on the business key, coalesce, and write.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: unionByName adds projection overhead but guarantees correctness; allowMissingColumns tolerates evolution but can mask missing data; distinct/dropDuplicates costs a shuffle but is required when sources overlap.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Read homogeneous sources with single glob reads to minimize union plan depth, push filters before union, coalesce to control partition count, and run the dedup shuffle once at the end rather than per source.

keyConcepts: union/unionAll = positional, UNION ALL, no dedup.
Output partitions = sum of input partitions; no shuffle for union itself.
interviewPoints: union matches by position, unionByName by name (column-order trap).
PySpark union is UNION ALL -- no dedup.
unionAll is a deprecated alias of union.
allowMissingColumns handles schema evolution by null-filling.
Union is a narrow transformation (no shuffle).
quickNotes: Default to unionByName unless schemas are guaranteed identical in order.
Add distinct() only when sources actually overlap.
Flatten many unions with reduce or a single glob read.
Coalesce after combining many sources to avoid tiny partitions.
Validate the resulting superset schema to catch silent drift.

keyTakeaways: `union` (and the deprecated `unionAll`) matches columns by POSITION while `unionByName` matches by NAME; the positional behavior silently corrupts data when columns are in a different order, so default to unionByName.
PySpark union is UNION ALL: it keeps all rows including duplicates, so you must explicitly call distinct() or dropDuplicates() -- which adds a shuffle -- when deduplication is required.

`unionByName(allowMissingColumns=True)` (Spark 3.1+) aligns by name and null-fills columns missing on either side, making it the safe choice for evolving schemas; plain union requires identical column counts and fails otherwise.

Union is a cheap narrow transformation with no shuffle, but its output partition count is the sum of the inputs, so combine many sources with reduce/glob reads and coalesce afterward to avoid plan bloat and tiny partitions.
The expensive part of a union pipeline is usually the optional dedup shuffle, not the union -- skip distinct() when sources are non-overlapping and run it once at the end when needed.
